title: Loop language: optimal counterexamples
description: The check prefers counterexamples with few relevant atoms (X + X = Z marks two numbers, X + Y = Z three).

fragments.name: shared
fragments.text:
% Rules every solver needs. The constant n is set in the Loop tab.
num(1..n).

fragments.name: abstraction
fragments.text:
% Solver A proposes candidates: here, any set of numbers.
{ pick(X) : num(X) }.
#show pick/1.

fragments.name: glue
fragments.text:
% The atoms solver A and solver C share. glue(T) makes T an interface atom:
% its value in a candidate is fixed when the check runs.
glue(pick(X)) :- num(X).
fragments.description: The interface atoms: every glue(T) makes T an interface atom.

fragments.name: check
fragments.text:
% Solver C looks for a counterexample: a sum X + Y = Z inside the candidate.
1 { sum(X,Y) : num(X), num(Y), X <= Y, X + Y <= n } 1.
:- sum(X,Y), not pick(X).
:- sum(X,Y), not pick(Y).
:- sum(X,Y), not pick(X+Y).
#show sum/2.

% relevant(T): the interface atoms the counterexample depends on.
% The refinement says: at least one of them must change.
relevant(pick(X)) :- sum(X,Y).
relevant(pick(Y)) :- sum(X,Y).
relevant(pick(X+Y)) :- sum(X,Y).

% Prefer counterexamples that mark few atoms.
#minimize { 1,T : relevant(T) }.
fragments.description: Looks for a counterexample to a candidate (solver C) and marks the atoms it depends on with relevant/1.

loop.text:
solver A = shared + abstraction
solver C = shared + check
link   G = A -> C via shared + glue

# With 'optimal', C.solve returns an optimal counterexample: here one that marks
# as few relevant atoms as possible (see the #minimize in the check fragment),
# which gives shorter refinement clauses.
search A:
    on candidate M:
        X = C.solve(assume G(M), optimal)
        if X:
            reject M with G.clause(M, X)
